Foreign Ownership of Condominiums in Thailand

The 49% quota, the money-transfer rule and what to check
HomeGuidesForeign Ownership of Condominiums in Thailand

Ownership and legal · Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Foreign buyers can own a condominium unit in Thailand in their own name, which is why most foreign purchases in Phuket are condos. Here are the main rules, in plain language.

The 49% foreign quota

Under the Condominium Act, foreign nationals and foreign-controlled entities may collectively own up to 49% of the total saleable area of a condominium building. The remaining 51% or more must be Thai-owned.

In practice a developer can sell foreign-quota units only until the quota is full. In a popular project, remaining foreign-quota units can run out, and some developers keep part of the quota for later phases. Ask for the current quota status in writing.

Funds must come from abroad

To register a condo transfer in a foreign buyer’s name, the purchase money is normally required to be remitted into Thailand in foreign currency. The receiving bank issues a foreign exchange transaction form, often called a FET or Tor Tor 3, and the Land Department asks for it at transfer.

Keep the bank documents. Money already held in a Thai baht account usually cannot be used to prove a foreign-quota purchase. Check the current requirement with your bank and lawyer before sending funds.

What you receive

A registered condo owner receives a title deed for the unit (a condominium title deed) and a share of the common property. Freehold is the term used for this type of ownership; see our freehold versus leasehold guide.

Checks before you reserve

  • Ask the developer for the foreign-quota availability in the building.
  • Verify the project’s licences, land title and developer track record.
  • Read the reservation and sale agreement, including delay and refund terms for off-plan units.
  • Ask which fees you will pay at transfer and who pays them.
  • Use an independent lawyer, not only the developer’s lawyer.

Off-plan and ready units

For off-plan projects you usually pay in instalments linked to construction and receive the title at completion. Ready units transfer after the sale agreement is signed. Our project pages state the construction status and, where the developer has published it, the payment plan.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a Thai bank account?

The foreign exchange transaction document comes from the bank receiving your transfer. Ask your bank and lawyer which account and documents are needed for your transfer.

Can a foreigner own more than 49% of a building?

No, not in aggregate. The 49% limit applies to the building as a whole.

General information only, not legal or tax advice, and rules can change. Confirm every point with a licensed Thai lawyer and the Land Department before you pay a deposit.

Sources: Thai Land Department, Bank of Thailand
